core: The electricity footprint of computing: data centers and networks as a growing share of global demand, with AI (and historically crypto) adding pressure
Data-center efficiency metrics, especially Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) and what it does not capture
Electronic waste: scale, low recycling rate, value of recoverable materials, and toxics/informal-recycling hazards
Green computing and sustainable design: efficient hardware, virtualization/cloud consolidation, device longevity, right to repair, responsible recycling and refurbishment
The honest tension that digital technology both enables efficiencies and consumes energy and materials
supporting: Distinction between operational and embedded (manufacturing) footprint
Distinction between electricity use and carbon intensity (grid dependence)
ENERGY STAR labeling as an efficiency program
outOfScope: The energy system as a whole (owned by the Energy Use topic)
General waste management and general recycling systems (owned by Waste Management and Recycling)
The circular-economy model in general (owned by Circular Economy; here applied specifically to electronics)
Detailed climate science, GHG accounting, or renewable-capacity figures

claims.claim: Data centers consumed about 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, roughly 1.5% of global electricity, and demand has grown about 12% per year since 2017 (over four times faster than total electricity).

The IEA projects data-center electricity use will more than double to about 945 TWh by 2030, with AI the most important driver; in 2024 the US accounted for ~45%, China ~25%, Europe ~15% of data-center electricity.
Cryptocurrency mining used about 110 TWh of electricity in 2022 (comparable to the Netherlands) and was projected by the IEA to rise toward about 160 TWh by 2026.

Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) is the ratio of total facility energy to IT-equipment energy, introduced by The Green Grid in 2007 and standardized as ISO/IEC 30134-2; 1.0 is ideal and higher values mean more overhead.
Reported industry-average PUE has been near 1.5-1.6 in recent years (Uptime Institute 2024 survey ~1.56), while the most efficient large operators report values near 1.1.
The world generated 62 million tonnes of e-waste in 2022, growing ~2.6 Mt/year and projected to reach 82 million tonnes by 2030; it is rising about five times faster than documented recycling.
Only 22.3% of 2022 e-waste was formally collected and recycled, a rate projected to decline toward 20% by 2030.
Metals embedded in 2022 e-waste were worth about US$91 billion, with about US$62 billion in recoverable resources unrecovered; only ~1% of rare-earth demand is met through recycling.
About 18 million tonnes of e-waste are handled by the informal sector in low- and middle-income countries, where crude recovery releases hazardous substances such as lead and mercury.

The FTC's 2021 report Nixing the Fix catalogued repair restrictions (parts limited to authorized networks, adhesives/designs resisting disassembly, software locks) and found scant evidence they are necessary for safety or security.

Because a large share of a device's footprint is embedded in manufacturing, extending device life through repair often reduces total impact more than early replacement, which is the sustainability case behind right-to-repair and refurbishment.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Projected data-center electricity demand varies across IEA reports and scenarios.
positions: IEA Electricity 2024 projected data-center total (incl. crypto/AI) exceeding 1,000 TWh by 2026 from ~460 TWh in 2022.
IEA Energy and AI (2025) reports ~415 TWh for data centers in 2024 and projects ~945 TWh by 2030.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Definitions and boundaries differ (e.g., inclusion of crypto, base year). The lesson uses the more recent 2025 Energy and AI figures for the headline data-center numbers and cites the 2024 report only for the crypto-specific figure, dating each.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only boilerplate ('a foundational concept... introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it') with no factual content about computing sustainability; nothing in it was usable as evidence.

Read the IEA executive summary and 'energy demand from AI' pages directly. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Electricity 2024 — Executive Summary
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the cryptocurrency figures: ~110 TWh in 2022 (comparable to the Netherlands) rising toward ~160 TWh by 2026, and the combined data-center/AI/crypto doubling narrative. Verified via IEA summary and corroborating reporting; used only for the crypto-specific and combined-forecast figures.

sourceRecords.title: The Global E-waste Monitor 2024
sourceRecords.notes: Intergovernmental report (ITU/UNITAR). Supports: 62 Mt e-waste in 2022; ~2.6 Mt/yr growth; 82 Mt projected by 2030; rising ~5x faster than recycling; 22.3% documented collection/recycling in 2022 (projected to fall to ~20% by 2030); ~US$91B metals value, ~US$62B unrecovered; ~1% of rare-earth demand met by recycling; ~18 Mt handled informally in low/middle-income countries with lead/mercury hazards. Read via the official ewastemonitor.info and UNITAR press release. Figures cited; no substantial text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Nixing the Fix: An FTC Report to Congress on Repair Restrictions (May 2021)
sourceRecords.notes: U.S. federal government work (public domain). Supports the right-to-repair discussion: manufacturer restrictions (parts limited to authorized networks, adhesives/designs resisting disassembly, software locks/DRM) and the finding of scant evidence that such restrictions are necessary for safety or security. Read the FTC report landing page and PDF.
